title: Opportunity makes opinion leaders: analyzing the role of first-hand information in opinion leadership in social media networks
central_claims: COP21 attendees identified by geolocation have higher Twitter network centrality, brokerage, activity and retweets than the average conference-hashtag user.

Access to first-hand information can enable opinion leadership without relying on traditional media. The cross-sectional study does not measure direct persuasion or persistence, and cannot fully establish causal effects.

source_manifest.title: Two sides of the same leader: an agent-based model to analyze the effect of ambivalent opinion leaders in social networks
source_manifest.finding: Röchert, Cargnino and Neubaum accurately discuss the COP21 political-actor result and distinguish diffusion-based influence from psychological opinion change. Their model does not reproduce the first-hand-information attendance result.

source_manifest.title: Teachers in the era of digitalization: use of social media in Latin-America
source_manifest.scope: abstract, methods, results and discussion through page18
source_manifest.finding: Vaillant, Marcelo and Marcelo-Martínez explicitly base an interview guide on Walter and Brüggemann’s conceptualization. They apply it to educational reference figures in Spain and Uruguay, collecting qualitative evidence about content creation, first-hand information and interactions. This demonstrates conceptual reuse, not replication of the COP21 causal interpretation.

answers.rationale: The education study applies the conceptualization but does not directly test whether first-hand access causes greater network influence; the simulation cites a subsidiary result.
Neither retrieved follow-up repeats the geolocated COP21 participant-versus-user design or independently reproduces its central result.
The education interviews ask different questions; they are not a stricter test of the attendance/first-hand-information claim.
Positive conceptual use is evident, but no authoritative critical assessment explicitly retains the complete central claim.
No retrieved study resolves the original geolocation selection, cross-sectional persistence or direct-opinion-influence limitations.
The education project applies the conceptualization; a substantive extension of the specific first-hand-access mechanism is not clearly established.

The 2025 study explicitly bases its educational-influencer interview guide on Walter and Brüggemann’s conceptualization; this is actual research use beyond citation.

search_gaps: No exact replication or explicit critical assessment of the first-hand-information effect was found. General opinion-leader citations are not automatically outcomes.
The paper appeared online in 2018 and in a 2020 journal issue. Later sources cite it as 2020; the assignment retains 2018.
Original main text and appendix read without truncation; bibliography not exhaustively reviewed. Follow-up reading scopes are specified for each source.
The five supported items share one primary follow-up source and are correlated dimensions of its reuse, not five independent confirmations.
research.summary: Independent researchers used the conceptualization to design educational-influencer interviews in 2025. This establishes bounded research utility and late reuse, but neither the simulation discussion nor the education study independently reproduces the central COP21 first-hand-information claim.
